Insolence

IN-suh-lens -- from Latin insolentia, from insolens ('unaccustomed, arrogant'), in- ('not') + solere ('to be accustomed'). · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Insolence is disrespectful and rude behavior, especially toward someone in a position of authority.

During the trial, the defendant's open insolence -- interrupting the proceedings and scoffing at every ruling -- nearly resulted in a contempt charge.

Worked Example

The knight's insolence toward the queen -- refusing to bow and openly mocking her decree in front of the court -- led to his banishment.

That open, deliberate disrespect directed at someone who is owed basic courtesy -- a teacher, a boss, an elder -- is exactly what insolence describes.

How Insolence Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

impertinence

impertinence: rude behavior that oversteps what is appropriate

impudence

impudence: bold, disrespectful behavior showing no shame

Antonyms

deference

deference: respectful submission to someone's wishes or authority

courtesy

courtesy: polite, respectful behavior toward others

How Strong Is It? — impertinence → insolence → impudence

impertinence vs. insolence

impertinence vs. insolence: The waiter's mild impertinence -- correcting the customer's order out loud -- earned him a stern look from the manager.

impudence vs. insolence

impudence vs. insolence: Nobody could believe the impudence of the freshman who put his feet up on the principal's desk.

Sort It Out

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: not (Latin)

root — sol-

root — sol-: to be accustomed, used to (Latin (solere))

suffix — -ence

suffix — -ence: state or quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Insolence combines in- ('not') with Latin solere ('to be accustomed') and -ence ('state or quality of') -- insolent behavior is literally 'unaccustomed' behavior, breaking the normal, expected rules of respect.

Use the root in a new word: obsolete

Use the root in a new word: obsolete: You may remember obsolete from earlier in this course -- ob- + solere means 'no longer practiced or in use,' the same root as insolence, just pointed at outdated things instead of rude people.
